blocks.text: **The problem.** Given a collection of numbers `nums` that **might contain duplicates**, return all **unique** permutations in any order.

blocks.alt: Permutations of 1, 1 and 2. Call the two ones 1 and 1-prime. Choosing 1-prime when the first 1 is unused would build the same permutations as choosing the first 1, so that branch is skipped. The three unique permutations are 112, 121 and 211.

elements.text: equal values are used in order: 1' only after the first 1 is already placed
elements.originalText: equal values are used in order: 1' only after the first 1 is already placed

blocks.text: The idea: use equal values in a fixed order

Duplicates appear because the two 1s can swap places and still give the same list. Fix that by agreeing to use equal values **in their sorted order**: sort the array, and allow `nums[i]` only if it differs from `nums[i − 1]` **or** `nums[i − 1]` is already used. The check is `if (i > 0 && nums[i] === nums[i − 1] && !used[i − 1]) continue`. Then among equal values, the first unused one is always the one placed — every distinct permutation is built exactly once.
**Time O(n · n!), space O(n · n!)** for the set. With many duplicates it builds far more than it keeps — `[1,1,1,1,1,1,1,2]` makes 40,320 lists to keep 8.

blocks.caption: A value equal to the one before it may only be placed after that one is already in the path.

blocks.text: **Time O(n · n!)** in the worst case (all distinct), but proportional to the number of **unique** permutations when there are duplicates. **Space O(n).**

rows.timeWhy: All **n!** orderings are built, each in O(n), even the repeats.
n! at worst, but only **unique** permutations are built when there are duplicates.

items: **Forgetting to sort** — the `a[i] === a[i − 1]` check needs equal values side by side.
**`!used[i − 1]` vs `used[i − 1]`** — both versions are correct (they keep the first or the last copy in place), but mixing them up with the Subsets II rule is a classic bug.
**Next Permutation** — the C++ version above uses it to step through unique permutations in order.
**Palindrome Permutation II** — build half the palindrome with unique permutations, then mirror it.
